newsitem.title: DUBAI: FEATURE-UAE advertising industry has way to go.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-UAE advertising industry has way to go.

text.p: Sales promotions are a way of life in the oil-rich United Arab Emirates, where the glitter of gold and lure of fast cars are used by retailers to catch the eyes of prosperous consumers in the Gulf state's desert cities.
With wage-earners free from income tax and property rights for foreigners restricted, consumption is a way of life for many who live in the UAE, one of the World Bank's 10 wealthiest countries.

But the advertising industry in the seven-state federation is still in its infancy and there are few sustained media campaigns to build brand recognition and product loyalty on goods such as vehicles, electronics and cosmetics.

"The fact that a lot of retail advertisers in the emirates use endless promotions is a sign of the low standards of advertising and marketing insight," said Edward Jones, chairman and executive creative director of Dubai-based Saatchi & Saatchi Advertising Middle East.
"The promotions are almost indistinguishable...they should be developing brands. It's very amateurish," Jones said.
Retailers, faced with an expatriate-dominated population of 2.4 million people who have stark income disparities, rely heavily on "buy one - win one" promotions to drum up business.
Many in the country's workforce, particularly from the Indian subcontinent and Asia, regularly send part of their wage packets home to support relatives.
Department stores, jewellers and fast-food outlets lead the cornucopia of prizes offered to entice customers to buy anything from diamond-studded watches to ice cream.
Eating at Kentucky Fried Chicken restaurants opens the way to win airline tickets to India while simply subscribing to a local newspaper can get you five grams of 24-carat Swiss gold.
In one of Dubai's many air-conditioned marble shopping malls, Marlboro cigarettes are promoted by the chance to win a sporty four-wheel-drive desert car.
Meanwhile rival Benson and Hedges hid special gold wrappers in some of its packets, giving the finder the right to a 10-gram piece of gold.

Though the UAE has an official per capita income of $14,000 -- one of the highest in the Arab world -- and is home to a wide range of television, radio and newspapers, spending by media advertisers is modest.
Per capita advertising spent in the country runs at just $67, compared with $321 in the United States, according to Ramzi Raad, executive vice-president of Intermarkets Group.
Just $150 million a year is spent on media advertising, according to the Pan Arab Research Centre.
But the prize draws show no signs of slowing down.
Even commercial banks and UAE airports offer sizeable rewards for opening accounts or buying duty free goods.

"I didn't even dream of winning. I just bought the certificates for the heck of it," Varghese Zacharia, a 35-year-old Indian pharmacist told a newspaper after winning the equivalent of $68,000 from a retail bank.
Local governments are also well versed in promoting their emirates, particularly in sport events ranging from cricket and to power-boat racing and horse racing.

Promotions in Dubai are set to reach a peak of frenzy next year when the city holds its second festival devoted entirely to shopping -- a 30-day campaign to boost sales in the emirate's shopping malls, gold and carpet souks.
